analysis.one_liner: Boosts low Social Security benefits and pays for it by taxing high wages above the cap.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in a Ways and Means subcommittee from April 2013 until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise Social Security benefits for the people the program serves worst: it would raise the special minimum benefit so that a worker with a long career could not retire below the poverty line, add a growing bonus for people who draw benefits for many years, and extend benefits to children of disabled or deceased workers through college at age 22. It would pay for this by gradually applying the Social Security payroll tax to wages above the annual cap (currently about $113,000) and by slowly raising the payroll tax rate from 6.2% to 6.5% for both workers and employers. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and then to its Social Security subcommittee, where it died without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners, whose minimum benefit would be tied to a percentage of the federal poverty line based on years worked (reaching 100% at 30 years); long-term beneficiaries, who would get an added amount starting 16 years after first qualifying and reaching 5% of an average earner's benefit after 20 years; and children of disabled or deceased workers attending college full-time, who would keep benefits to age 22 instead of losing them at 19. The bill also bars those benefit increases from being counted as income when someone applies for food stamps, Medicaid, or other aid, so the extra money is not taken away elsewhere.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low earners, long-term retirees, and students

how_it_helps.text: Raises the special minimum benefit so workers with at least 11 years of covered work receive a share of the poverty guideline, scaling up to the full amount at 30 or more years of work.
Adds a benefit increase for people who draw Social Security for a long time — starting at 16 years after first eligibility, phasing from 20% to 100% of a 5% add-on by year 20.
Extends child's benefits for full-time post-secondary students to age 22, for children of workers who were disabled or died fully insured.

Counts none of the new benefit increases as income or resources for any federal or federally funded state program, so the extra dollars are not clawed back through food stamps, Medicaid, or housing assistance.

analysis.who_pays: High earners whose wages exceed the annual payroll-tax cap would pay Social Security tax on the excess for the first time, with the taxable share rising from 90% in 2015 to all wages above the cap after 2024. Every worker and employer would also pay a higher payroll tax rate, phasing from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2020 (self-employed, from 12.4% to 13.0%), and high earners would also receive somewhat higher benefits from a new 3% benefit factor on earnings above the cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the tax cap, all employers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the employee and employer payroll tax rate on all wages from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2020, and the self-employment tax from 12.4% to 13.0% — a real cost to every covered worker and business, phased in from 2015.

It applies the Social Security tax to wages above the annual contribution and benefit base on a sliding schedule — 90% taxed in 2015, 50% in 2019, and 0% excluded after 2024 — so upper-income earners face a new tax on income that is currently capped.
The bill also adds a 3% benefit factor on earnings above the cap, meaning higher earners would earn somewhat larger benefits, partially offsetting the revenue raised from lifting the cap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is tightly targeted at people the current formula leaves behind: lifetime low earners, very long-term beneficiaries, and students who lost a parent. The costs are broad but modest for most people — about a 0.3-point payroll tax increase over five years — while the largest cost falls on wages above roughly $113,000 a year, which are currently exempt. The main honest objection is that raising everyone's payroll tax rate is regressive, hitting working-class paychecks, though the minimum benefit and long-duration increases push money back toward exactly those workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then to its Social Security subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore introduced the bill on March 21, 2013, with Rep. Jan Schakowsky as the only cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
On April 9, 2013, the committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Social Security, and the congressional record shows no further action for the remainder of the 113th Congress.
The Congress ended January 3, 2015, with the bill having never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners with wages above the payroll-tax cap, along with employers, are better off because the bill died: they continue to pay Social Security tax only up to the annual cap and avoid the phased-in rate increase. Social Security beneficiaries receive no new benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll cap

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Enhancement and Protection Act of 2013 in the House.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; referred the bill to its Social Security subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or vote
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the April 2013 subcommittee referral, leaving the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill, no Republican supported it, and the committee never brought it to a vote, so no roll call ever revealed the real split.

industries.industry: High earners with wages above the payroll-tax cap
industries.note: The bill would phase out the cap on wages subject to Social Security tax, reaching full taxation of wages above roughly $113,000 by 2025. Their new tax obligation is what funds the benefit increases for low and long-term beneficiaries.
The employer share of the Social Security tax would rise from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2020, and the employer tax would also apply to wages above the cap, raising labor costs slightly across the economy.
The self-employment tax rate would rise from 12.4% to 13.0% and apply to earnings above the cap, increasing what independent high earners owe.
